title: Books in your ears
text: Audiobooks were once an {{1}} for people who could not read print — cassettes in plastic cases, rented by post. They are now the fastest-growing format in publishing, and the industry's problem is finding enough narrators, not listeners. Something deeper than convenience is {{2}}. A skilled narrator {{3}} what the page leaves open: pace, irony, which line of dialogue is a joke. Some books {{4}} this treatment — complex timelines benefit from a voice that signals the shifts; others, dense with charts or wordplay that lives on the page, suffer. The nervousness of authors is {{5}}: writers report hearing their own novels with sudden, merciless clarity, and the best narrators come to {{6}} as co-authors, shaping character by vowels alone. Meanwhile the definition of reading is being renegotiated in public: purists insist the eyes-only version is the real one, while everyone else quietly {{7}} that a novel understood is a novel read, whatever carried it into the mind. Publishing, which once feared the audiobook would {{8}} the printed book, now treats it as its most loyal companion: formats, it turns out, grow together more often than they compete.

gaps.explanation: 'an accommodation for people who could not read print' — an arrangement meeting their need; accumulation = a pile-up.
'something deeper is operating' — is at work here; oppress = rule harshly, overlap = partly cover.

gaps.hint: fixes, resolves (what the page leaves open)
gaps.explanation: 'a narrator settles what the page leaves open' — decides it; rattle = shake noisily, shuttle = move back and forth.
'some books suit this treatment' — are well matched to it; suite = a set of rooms or furniture, sue = take legal action.
'the nervousness of authors is understandable' — easy to see why; unjustified and unnecessary contradict the sympathy of the passage.
'come to count as co-authors' — 'count as' = be treated as; amount takes 'to', account takes 'for'.
'everyone else quietly agrees that…' — accepts the view; allude = refer to indirectly, allay = calm a fear.
'feared the audiobook would cannibalise the printed book' — the business term for one product eating another's sales; condone = overlook a fault.
